title: Registry models link prescribing patterns to clinic and medication context
summary: In 864,339 registry patients with atrial fibrillation, an enhanced XGBoost model identified documented anticoagulant prescriptions with a test AUROC of0.811. Clinic-location income, clinic size and region contributed permutation importance alongside age and concurrent medications. These are descriptive prescribing-pattern associations, not causal socioeconomic effects.
ai_technology: XGBoost; random forest; penalized logistic regression
organization: Stanford University; American College of Cardiology

source_review.scope: Official primary BioC original article sections: Registry/outcome/feature Methods;patient split/tuning;test permutation-importance Results and limitations; no laboratory-method validation

evidence.ai_role: Fitted classifiers map patient and clinic features to documented prescriptions. Permutation analysis on the test set identifies model-used contextual information beyond a clinical risk-score feature set.
evidence.tested: PINNACLE records from January2017–June2018 were split80:20 by patient; hyperparameters used fivefold training cross-validation. Prescription status and inputs came from the most recent three-month record window.
evidence.unknown: Income is a clinic-ZIP-code mean, not each patient’s household income. Concurrent medications and INR can reflect prescribing or monitoring consequences rather than causes; same-clinic records can occur on both sides of the random split. Missing fields and voluntary outpatient practices limit representativeness. The CHA2DS2-VASc comparator is a clinical stroke-risk score, not a prescription model; no causal disparity, guideline benefit or improved treatment outcome is established.
